entries.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
entries.summary: This second installment reviews 13 more Amazon SageMaker AI inference launches from 2026, spanning configuration recommendations, fitting more models onto each GPU, serving models too large for one instance, cross-Region routing, and post-launch tuning, bringing the year's total to 26.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2

Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.

For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway delivers the routing, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.

To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.

The launches at a glance

Choose the right configuration from wherever you work

The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.

Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.

Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026)

Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI

The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.

SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.

Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026)

Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK

Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.

The SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.

LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026)

Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters

Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.

Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, update, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.

SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026)

Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI

Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.

Inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set 

search_recipe
to 
max-concurrency-under-sla
and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (
feasible_max
) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (
infeasible_min
).

The search uses the same 

CreateAIWorkloadConfig
and 
CreateAIBenchmarkJob
APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (
concurrency_min
, 
concurrency_max
, 
search_max_iterations
, and 
search_initial_points
) bound the cost and speed up convergence.

Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026)

Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent

Engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.

The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:

  • Find the right instance. Ranked deployment options with measured throughput, latency, and TTFT for a model in Amazon S3, SageMaker JumpStart, or the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Benchmark a live endpoint. A report from real load covering throughput, P50 and P99 latency, inter-token latency, and supported concurrency.
  • Compare runs. The percentage change on every metric, which shows whether a configuration change helped.

Answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.

For the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.

Fit more models onto each GPU

The support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.

Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026)

With Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.

In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, update, and delete inference components:

  • Create and edit. Create an endpoint with inference components, add or delete components later, and change each component’s accelerators, CPU, memory, and copy count.
  • Scale each model. Set an automatic scaling policy for each component, down to zero copies, so an idle model stops holding accelerators.
  • Monitor. See alarms and per-component metrics on the same page.

The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.

GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (October 2026)

Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.

MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.

For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.

Serve models larger than one instance

The team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.

Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026)

Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.

With this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:

  • Capacity and networking. GPU capacity and EFA networking, provisioned and wired automatically.
  • Node recovery. Node health monitoring and replacement, with multi-node workers rescheduled automatically when a node fails.
  • Endpoint operations. Autoscaling, endpoint registration, TLS, and observability.
  • One install and upgrade path. The Inference Operator add-on installs Dynamo, the serving images, and the Grove and KAI schedulers as one unit and upgrades them together.

The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:

  • Multi-node (sharded) serving. One copy of the model spans several nodes, so you can serve models that do not fit on any single instance.
  • Disaggregated prefill and decode. Prompt processing and token generation run on separate GPU pools, each on an instance type suited to its work, so a long prompt no longer slows responses for other users.
  • KV-aware routing. Each request goes to the worker that already holds its KV cache, which reduces TTFT.

There are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing 

DynamoGraphDeployment
(DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can update the add-on and add a short 
dynamoSpec
block to an existing 
InferenceEndpointConfig
, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.

Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

For the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.

Send each request to a GPU that can serve it

The support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.

Routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the launches below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.

KV-cache-aware routing for endpoints (November 2026)

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

Applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.

KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.

It works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports 

InvokeEndpoint
, 
InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream
, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.

Which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over quickly.

Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026)

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway

Inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, new requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.

The Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:

  • KV cache utilization. Avoids pods whose cache is nearly full.
  • Queue depth and running requests. Avoids pods with a backlog and balances active work.
  • Prefix cache hit rate. Prefers pods likely to hold the prompt prefix.
  • LoRA adapter residency. Prefers pods that already hold the requested adapter, which avoids swap latency.

Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Cross-Region Inference Routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

On managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.

The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:

  • One invocation path. SageMaker tries the local endpoint first and moves traffic to another registered endpoint when the local one cannot serve a request.
  • One routing policy. The policy combines endpoint metrics with service-side capacity signals, including insufficient capacity errors that customers cannot observe on their own.
  • Private connectivity. Cross-Region traffic runs over AWS PrivateLink with a managed cross-account authorization model, so routing to another Region or account does not need internet or NAT gateways.
  • Overflow and residency guardrails. The endpoint owner can cap how much cross-Region traffic a fallback endpoint accepts, and the application can restrict which Regions may serve a request.

Keep endpoints tuned after launch

Two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.

Continuous performance monitoring (November 2026)

Amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.

There are three types of findings:

  • Latency drift after a traffic change. When a change such as added retrieval lengthens prompts, TTFT rises. The finding quantifies the regression week over week and recommends re-running inference recommendations against recent traffic to find a configuration that brings TTFT back down.
  • A configuration gap present since deployment. The endpoint was never well tuned for its workload, and the finding points to the change that would close the gap.
  • Idle GPU capacity. When capacity stays unused week after week, the finding flags a chance to right-size the endpoint and reduce cost.

In-place rolling model updates (November 2026)

A standard rolling update replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding new capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.

SageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The update still rolls out in stages, but it needs new capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.

For the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a new recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.

Summary: 13 launches, continuing from part 1

The numbering continues from the 13 launches in part 1.

14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.

15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.

16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.

17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.

18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.

19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.

20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.

21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.

22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.

23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.

24. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.

25. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.

26. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.

By the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.

Part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 13 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.

What is next

On managed endpoints, we plan to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model update.

Documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.

References

  • Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review
  • New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent
  • Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway
  • What’s New: GPU partitioning for SageMaker AI

entries.title: Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 adds a native Amazon Bedrock provider, so you can connect the open source coding agent to models like Kimi K3.1 Pro using your standard AWS credential chain (named profiles or SSO) instead of a separate API key. This post shows how to configure the provider and send your first request.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock

Kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect.

With v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key.

In this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling.

What’s new

Amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs. Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model.

In older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with 

type = "openai"
or 
type = "openai_responses"
. These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional 
base_url
and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key. The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage.

The native provider changes that setup:

  • Use your existing AWS authentication workflow. The 
    bedrock
    provider can resolve temporary credentials through the standard AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) credential chain. You can use the default chain or select a named profile, including a profile backed by SSO.
  • Override the protocol for each model, if needed. The provider infers an API format and regional endpoint from the model ID, but you can change them as detailed in the “Override endpoint URL and protocol” section of this post.

AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This new path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately.

How it works

The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps:

  • Resolve AWS credentials. Unless you configure an Amazon Bedrock API key, the bedrock provider uses the standard AWS credential chain in your environment. You can set 
    AWS_PROFILE
    to select a specific named profile.
  • Generate a short-lived bearer token. The provider uses @aws/bedrock-token-generator to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, and renews it when necessary. You don’t need to place any AWS access key or manually generated Amazon Bedrock key in the Kimi Code 
    config.toml
    . However, an explicit key given through 
    api_key
    or 
    api_key_env
    takes precedence if you provide it.
  • Build the regional endpoint. The provider resolves 
    AWS_REGION
    or 
    AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
    and constructs the appropriate 
    bedrock-runtime
    endpoint for the model’s inferred API. For Kimi models, this resolves to the recommended OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions path.
  • Call the selected inference profile. The model alias maps to an Amazon Bedrock model or inference profile ID. This example uses the global inference profile 
    global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1
    . The 
    global.
    prefix selects the profile, while 
    AWS_REGION
    determines the regional endpoint that receives your request.

The CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. The ephemeral API keys generated by the provider are valid for up to 12 hours or your AWS session length, whichever is shorter.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, we use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example model, accessed through global cross-Region inference for broadest availability and lowest cost. Review the Amazon Bedrock pricing to understand expected costs before using the model.

To follow along, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to the target model and inference profile in a supported source AWS Region. Check the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model card for current Region and inference-profile support.
  • Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 or later. Follow the Kimi Code CLI installation guide and run 
    kimi --version
    to check your installation.
  • The AWS CLI, to follow the profile and identity-check commands in this post. The optional 
    aws login
    workflow requires AWS CLI v2.32.0 or later.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity (user or assumed role) with permissions to invoke the target model and inference profile in your chosen AWS Region.

The following example IAM policy grants the permissions used by this walkthrough, for the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model and global inference profile only. Replace 

${AWS_REGION}
with your source Region (for example, 
us-west-2
for US West Oregon) and 
${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}
with your 12-digit AWS account ID:

The foundation-model ARN without a Region or account ID is intentional and required for global cross-Region routing. The 

BedrockInvokeKimiK31DefaultProject
statement is only required if using the 
openai_responses
protocol, not with the default 
openai
(Chat Completions).

Security of your AWS environment is a shared responsibility. Review and grant IAM permissions according to the principle of least privilege, particularly for production environments. Consider using a dedicated IAM role for Kimi Code CLI, separate from your regular AWS activities.

Get started with the 
bedrock
provider

After your prerequisites are ready, follow these steps to configure AWS authentication, add the provider and model, and send a test request.

Step 1: Configure AWS credentials

There are different ways to authenticate with the AWS CLI, depending on your organization’s setup. With Named profiles, you can configure multiple AWS contexts and switch between them.

For example:

  • If you use SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center, run 
    aws configure sso --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME
    to set up a profile, then run 
    aws sso login --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME
    to authenticate.
  • To use AWS Management Console credentials with AWS CLI v2.32.0 or later, run 
    aws login --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME
    . The console-credential login guide also describes a 
    credential_process
    configuration for tools that don’t support the cached login session directly.
  • Omit the 
    --profile
    arguments to use your default AWS profile instead of a named one.

Whichever approach you choose, your session resolves to an IAM identity (user or role) that needs the Amazon Bedrock permissions from the prerequisites. A Region configured in an AWS CLI profile applies to AWS CLI commands, but you must still set the Region explicitly for Kimi Code in Step 2.

Verify that the AWS CLI resolves your intended identity. Omit 

--profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME
if you use the default profile:

Step 2: Add the provider and model

  • Open or create 
    ~/.kimi-code/config.toml
    in a text editor. If you set 
    KIMI_CODE_HOME
    , use 
    $KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml
    instead. If you have an existing file, back it up and merge these entries with your current settings rather than overwriting unrelated providers or models.
  • Replace 
    YOUR_SOURCE_REGION
    with your supported source Region (for example, 
    us-west-2
    ). To use a named profile, replace 
    YOUR_PROFILE_NAME
    and uncomment the 
    AWS_PROFILE
    line:

    The model alias 

    bedrock-kimi-k3-1
    is a local name used by Kimi Code CLI. The model value is the Amazon Bedrock global inference-profile ID. The example declares a 1-million-token context window and explicit reasoning, image-input, and tool-use capabilities. It omits 
    api_key
    , 
    api_key_env
    , and 
    AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK
    , so the provider uses ambient AWS credentials. A configured Amazon Bedrock key would take precedence.
  • Save the file. The 
    [providers.bedrock.env]
    table supplies configuration to the provider. It doesn’t export variables into your shell.

Step 3: Send a request and start a coding session

  • Run a small non-interactive coding request:
  • Confirm that the CLI streams a response without an authentication, authorization, Region, model-access, or network error. This request provides a more meaningful connectivity check than a provider status indicator.
  • Start an interactive session in a project directory:

    Because you set 

    default_model
    , the session selects 
    bedrock-kimi-k3-1
    automatically. Ask the agent to explain the repository or propose a small change. Review its proposed file modifications and shell commands before approving them.

Configuration best practices

At the time of writing, the native bedrock provider has several configuration considerations. These practices help you avoid ambiguous status information and mismatched settings.

Use the configuration file to set up the provider

At the time of writing, Kimi Code’s desktop and web provider-creation interfaces don’t expose all the provider environment fields used by this credential-chain setup. Edit 

config.toml
directly to set up the Amazon Bedrock provider. For further details, refer to Model providers in the Kimi Code documentation.

Declare model capabilities explicitly

Kimi Code doesn’t auto-detect the capabilities of most models on Amazon Bedrock, including Kimi models. Check the Amazon Bedrock model card for each target model and explicitly declare its capabilities to let Kimi Code make use of them.

For example, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports 

always_thinking
, 
thinking
, 
image_in
, and 
tool_use
, but not 
audio_in
or 
video_in
, as reflected in the 
config.toml
example shown earlier.

These declarations describe client behavior. You should only include capabilities that are supported for each target model and Amazon Bedrock API endpoint. Validate tool and image workflows for your application rather than relying on the capability labels alone.

Keep Region settings consistent and prefer cross-Region inference where possible

The bedrock provider requires an explicit 

AWS_REGION
or 
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
in Kimi Code’s 
config.toml
or the shell environment. It can’t infer a Region configured only in 
~/.aws/config
or through 
aws configure
.

When you use cross-Region inference profiles (with prefixes such as 

global.
, 
us.
, or 
in.
), the configured Kimi Code Region controls the source Region that receives your requests. For more information, refer to cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

For workloads without data-residency requirements, start with the global inference profile. This model, like many others, is priced 10% lower for global inference than through geographic profiles. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing for current rates and geographic alternatives.

Override endpoint URL and protocol where needed

In some cases, the provider’s auto-detection might mistake the API protocol or target URL you want to use for a particular model. For example, you will need to set a different URL to use Amazon Bedrock through a VPC endpoint or the Mantle endpoints.

In the Kimi Code 

config.toml
, you can:
  • Set the 
    protocol
    field to 
    openai
    (Chat Completions), 
    openai_responses
    , or 
    anthropic
    (Messages) to configure a model to use a particular supported wire protocol. See the model cards for which models support which APIs.
  • Set the 
    base_url
    field to change the target URL, which must include any attached API path like 
    /openai/v1
    or 
    /anthropic
    .

In the following example, we show a configuration to connect to the same model but using the OpenAI Responses API through an Amazon Bedrock VPC endpoint you’ve set up:

Treat connectivity status as a configuration indicator

In the Kimi Code desktop and web apps, the provider list can show 

connected
for a bedrock provider. That status doesn’t validate the configured AWS credentials, IAM permissions, Region, model access, or network path. Don’t treat it as proof of a successful model request. Use the non-interactive prompt to test the complete path, and diagnose the actual response if it fails.

Cleanup

If you created a new AWS IAM identity or assigned new permissions to experiment with Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, remember to delete them when you’re finished testing.

You might also want to revert any local Kimi Code CLI provider configurations or AWS CLI profiles you set up. You can even uninstall the CLIs altogether if they’re no longer required. See the uninstall guides for Kimi Code and AWS CLI for details. Remember that deleting the local AWS configuration or CLI doesn’t by itself revoke IAM permissions or an active AWS session.

Amazon Bedrock inference for the models we showed is charged on a per-token basis, so there’s no persistent cloud infrastructure deployment to clean up.

Conclusion

We showed how Moonshot AI’s native bedrock provider in Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 connects to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock through the standard AWS credential chain. You no longer need a separately managed Amazon Bedrock API key.

Amazon Bedrock gives you access to open and proprietary AI models from leading providers, through standard APIs. Its governance controls and compliance validation programs can support even strictly regulated workloads.

If you’re already using Kimi Code CLI and want to run inference on AWS, upgrade today and give the new streamlined authentication a try.

For more information about Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, see our launch blog post and the Moonshot AI on AWS samples repository. To explore supported APIs and features by model, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us.

entries.title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments now supports AWS Marketplace, so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled products, APIs, data, and content and pay in USD on the developer's AWS bill, with no stablecoin wallets or API keys. This post walks through a research agent that finds a tool, pays per request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments

When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace, so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys.

Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect.

The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them:

Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them.

That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale.

This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like.

— Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily

What’s launching today

Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill.

When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill.

To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID.

An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, agents can only buy the products it allows.

In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request.

In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account.

Sample walkthrough

Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was announced about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints.

The agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost.

In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use.

How it works

1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts.

2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the 

PAYMENT-REQUIRED
header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected.

3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the 

ProcessPayment
API with the payment type 
AWS_BILLING_X402
. If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged.

4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the 

PAYMENT-SIGNATURE
header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass.

5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and shows up in their AWS bill monthly.

Prerequisites

To create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce. AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details.

Hands-on

The open-source GitHub sample in the 

agentcore-samples
repository runs through a demo of the new functionality. It can help you configure AgentCore payments for AWS Marketplace, connect Tavily, run the agent, and inspect the transaction. You can refer to the documentation for more details.

Step 1: Configure AgentCore payments

setup_aws_billing.py
creates a payment manager with an AWS Billing connector, plus the AWS Marketplace service-linked role and three separate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. The session role can set budgets but can’t pay. Meanwhile the agent role can pay but can’t create sessions, so the agent has no way to raise its own budget.

Step 2: Connect Tavily

setup_gateway.py
creates an AgentCore Gateway with the AWS Marketplace connector and gives the agent role the appropriate permissions to use it. The gateway’s role is limited to three read-only AWS Marketplace actions. If you choose to skip this step, you can instead set 
SELLER_URL
in the environment variables to the seller’s endpoint, and the agent will pay that URL only rather than using AgentCore Gateway discovery.

Step 3: Run the agent

The script creates a payment session as the session role and then runs the agent as the agent role. By default the session budget is $0.05 and the per-request cap is $0.02.

The agent searches, looks at listings, gets an endpoint, and pays once. In this test run against a $0.01 seller, it compared two listings before buying:

Step 4: Inspect the transaction

When the run finishes, the sample will print the payment with its amount, AWS Marketplace product ID, and 

processPaymentId
. The AWS Marketplace meters charges asynchronously, so the Tavily line item takes a moment to appear on your bill. Agent purchases will also show up in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer.

Step 5: Clean up

Run 

cleanup.py
to delete resources. Make sure to validate deletion to avoid incurring additional resource charges.

Conclusion

AgentCore payments and AWS Marketplace provide the infrastructure for agents that can transact. The research agent in this post goes from “I need live web search” to sourcing an answer on its own, discovering premium paid content through tools, and paying for requests that settle on the developer’s AWS bill.

With AgentCore payments, developers can build with open protocols like x402, which opens them to a growing catalog of trusted, verified AWS Marketplace sellers. This gives agents more autonomy and developers more control. Governance is built in, with per-session spending caps and an approved seller list using AgentCore policy, and IAM identities that make it auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. The agent chooses the right tool for the task, and developers can keep the same billing, budgets, and controls they already trust.

entries.title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
entries.summary: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, governance cannot be an afterthought. The BMW Group shares the practices and patterns its R&D teams use to build, govern, and operate AI agents at enterprise scale without sacrificing speed, quality, or compliance.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers

When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought.

At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high.

While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge.

Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group.

In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance.

Solution

Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain.

Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation.

Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start.

We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity.

Govern proactively, not retroactively

Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance:

Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations.

Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels:

  • Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop): Every action requires explicit human approval. This is the starting point for new agents and high-risk operations.
  • Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop): The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review. Suitable for medium-risk tasks with defined inputs, outputs, and rollback options.
  • Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails): The agent operates independently within strictly defined policy boundaries, enforced deterministically rather than through prompt instructions (see below). Reserved for low-risk, well-understood operations with verified track records.

Assign trust levels per step, not per agent. A single workflow can include steps at all three levels, so teams can start conservatively and incrementally increase autonomy as confidence builds, grounded in measurable evaluation data, not assumptions.

Deterministically enforced: Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop. In practice, this happens mainly in the CI/CD pipeline. Permission checks, policy-as-code rules, and compliance validations gate every deployment there, before an agent reaches production. Because these checks run separately from the agent, neither the agent nor its prompts are in a position to override them. Egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning) help prevent an agent holding confidential data from disclosing it through an otherwise legitimate call.

Instrument, verify, and evaluate continuously

Observability in agentic systems goes beyond traditional application monitoring. The real question is no longer whether a service returned an HTTP 200 status, but whether an agent produced a faithful, policy-compliant output, and how this can be demonstrated through observable execution traces. Answering that requires a ground-truth dataset covering common queries and edge cases. This dataset is used for evaluation from day one, so quality is measured against representative and appropriately governed evaluation datasets for evaluation, not synthetic prompts.

This infrastructure cannot be retrofitted and must be part of the initial design. The continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline enforces this, so agents lacking instrumentation fail validation before evaluation runs.

We recommend instrumenting three dimensions:

  • Intent tracing: Capture the observable agent trajectory (reasoning steps, tool invocations, and context retrievals) for each execution. OpenTelemetry spans create a queryable lineage from user request to final output.
  • Verification and evaluation as CI: Any change to the agent (prompt edits, tool additions, model swaps) triggers the pipeline. Verification runs first with automated regression tests covering agent components and then their interactions. As most harness components are deterministic, these tests are fast and fully automatable. Evaluation runs second, scoring non-deterministic output against the ground-truth dataset, gated on quality thresholds. This sequencing is deliberate: Verification acts as a gate, so evaluations only run on a passing build.
  • Model tiering and routing telemetry: When agents route between models, capture the routing decision and its justification, not just the outcome. Tier assignments are derived from evaluation results per task type and poor outcomes flow back as new evaluation cases.

Start focused, design for composition

For distributed cloud systems, the industry solved the complexity of end-to-end workflows by adopting architectural patterns such as microservices or service meshes. The evolution of agentic systems needs to follow a similar trajectory, moving from monolithic, generalist agents toward multiple collaborating specialized agents.

Teams should define the problem before considering agents’ functionality. Before writing any orchestration logic, they should produce five concrete artifacts:

  • Clear scope definition: what the agent should and shouldn’t do.
  • Interaction model: how users and other agents will invoke it.
  • Unambiguous tool definitions: each tool and parameter precisely defined.
  • Ground-truth dataset: the evaluation reference described above, established before any implementation begins.
  • Evaluation criteria: quality thresholds and benchmarks the agent will be measured against.

This discipline prevents the most common failure modes we observe: agents that take on too many responsibilities accumulate bloated prompts, reducing accuracy and increasing latency.

Once a single agent is well-scoped, it must be designed as a composable building block. Therefore, we define a three-tier composition hierarchy:

  • MCP tools are atomic integration contracts. Each tool wraps a single capability (for example, an API call or a database query) without encoding workflow assumptions. This is the stable, reusable layer.
  • Skills are bundled, domain-specific compositions of MCP tools. A code review skill, for example, might chain a static analysis tool, a style-check tool, and an LLM-based reasoning step. Skills encode domain logic but remain portable across workflows.
  • Flows are end-to-end orchestrations of skills, representing complete business processes (for example, an entire PR review pipeline or a requirements-to-deployment cycle).

Each tier is validated independently in the CI/CD pipeline. Component tests cover tools and skills, interaction tests cover their composition into flows.

These tiers are connected through open standards: MCP and Agent Skills for tool integration, the protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and OpenTelemetry for observability across the resulting interactions.

Figure 1 shows how the three tiers build on each other, from individual MCP tools at the base to complete flows at the top.

Specialize as you learn

In production, even well-scoped agents can break down as real-world usage diverges from what was anticipated at design time: query patterns shift, tool-selection logic struggles, and performance degrades unpredictably.

The right response is to decompose complex agents into multiple specialized ones, each with clearer instructions, simpler tool sets, and more focused reasoning. The benefits are concrete:

  • Evolve independently: updating a requirements engineering agent does not require touching the coding agent.
  • Scale individually: when scope and interfaces are well-defined, individual agents can be scaled independently without redeploying or resizing the broader system.
  • Minimized scope: a failure or hallucination of one agent does not cascade across the entire workflow.
  • Cost savings: A narrowly scoped agent can often run on a smaller model, which cuts inference and hosting costs.

Complexity can be reduced along two axes:

  • Within an agent: decompose capabilities into skills since tools and few-shot examples consume context on every invocation while degrading accuracy and increasing cost. Determine granularity empirically: merge skills the agent rarely selects and split skills that produce different behavior depending on the input.
  • Across agents: delegate work outside an agent’s domain to a specialized peer over the A2A protocol rather than extending the current agent. An agent should grow in capability, not in context.

Critically, since each specialized agent only accesses the data and tools required for its role, this architecture helps to enforce least-privilege by design, a compliance requirement in regulated industries.

Realizing these benefits, however, requires that agents can find and interoperate with each other. To prevent the emergence of AI islands, we maintain a centralized registry of agents, tools, and skills. This registry serves as:

  • Discovery mechanism: cataloging available agents, tools, and skills based on metadata stored during build.
  • Governance checkpoint: confirming approval of the asset types for production use and maintaining an audit trail.
  • Security checkpoint: automated security checks are applied before approval, such as prompt injection and similar issues.
  • Deduplication safeguard: identifying equivalent capabilities already maintained by other teams to avoid duplicate work. This check runs automatically at registration, flagging duplicates before approval.

Scale through codification

The shift from managing individual agents to governing an agent fleet requires agent architectures to be codified. Using Infrastructure-as-code frameworks such as Terraform or AWS CloudFormation, teams provision and manage agent infrastructure with the same rigor applied to any production system:

  • Fine-grained least-privilege roles: scoped per agent or tool.
  • CI/CD pipelines: consistent, validated deployments across accounts and regions, with automated deployment stops on failed tests or metric deterioration.
  • Policy-as-code: rules (for example, AWS Config, Open Policy Agent) scanning deployed agents for compliance with organizational standards.

All three are enforced as pipeline gates, validated before registration, not audited after the fact.

The adoption model is deliberately bottom-up with central curation. Individual teams build skills and MCP tools to solve their immediate problems. All teams can contribute by sharing their assets through the registry. A central team builds automatic governance checks as part of the CI pipeline to uphold standards. To support development teams and foster shift-left, the central team additionally provides building blocks as governance-as-code modules.

This balance avoids both centrally mandated architectures and unmanaged experimentation. As a result, when new operational concerns arise, teams can extend existing patterns rather than redesign their architectures.

Operationalizing best practices across the agent lifecycle

Architectural patterns and governance standards are only effective if they are embedded into the workflows teams use to build and operate agents before and at runtime.

Before deployment

Governance begins before a single line of orchestration logic is written. Teams are provided with reference architecture patterns and examples drawn from the registry. These pre-validated blueprints cover common agent configurations, tool integration patterns, and composition structures, which accelerate development while encoding proven defaults. Before anything reaches production, standardized CI/CD controls enforce these practices. Figure 2 shows the four phases of a reference pipeline, which run in order from left to right.

Phase 1 from Figure 2 runs fast, deterministic checks: supply chain security (approved registries only), component and interaction testing, evaluation library references, and observability instrumentation.

Phase 2 runs security and governance checks in parallel. Static analysis scans the code for issues, and security tests probe the agent in an isolated staging environment. The pipeline also validates egress controls and least-privilege permissions. Two more checks confirm that the agent’s declared autonomy level matches its actual permissions and that its configuration passes the policy-as-code rules. A governance agent accelerates audits by checking the agent against established standards and flagging findings for human review, such as:

  • Scope creep: operating beyond originally defined purpose or permissions.
  • Prompt bloat: unnecessary complexity in instructions.
  • Tool misuse: calling tools outside their intended use case.
  • Performance degradation: declining accuracy, latency, or cost-efficiency.

Figure 3: Example governance agent workflow

This assessment surfaces concrete, actionable measures that teams can apply immediately, rather than abstract recommendations. Figure 3 shows the governance agent’s dashboard for an agent maturity assessment. The governance agent provides evidence and actionable recommendations, while accountable humans own governance decisions. Recommendations require human confirmation before being applied, maintaining a four-eyes principle for accountability. Findings update the agent’s governance status in the registry, while full details are logged separately in a central knowledge base for audit and traceability.

Phase 3 evaluates the agent as a running system: the ground-truth evaluation gate (scores outputs against benchmarks established at design time) and agent performance (latency, token consumption). Figure 4 details the metrics, scoring criteria and the relationships between them.

Phase 4 checks for duplicates before registering the agent, its sub-agents, tools, and skills. The following table shows the metadata fields stored per agent in the registry.

Agent metadata
Core data:
  • unique identifier
  • name
  • description
  • version
  • business owner
  • IT owner
  • Capabilities: names, descriptions
  • Functions list: name, description, direction: provides/ uses
  • Status: plan / active / deprecated
  • Link to specification, agent card or documentation
  • Hosting mode: on-prem, cloud, cloud-region
Service level agreement data:
  • Target availability in percent
  • Target P95 response time in ms
  • Support hours / operational support model
Data governance flags:
  • information classification level
  • personal data processed flag
  • data retention period/ policy
  • request and response payloads logged flag
  • PII data redacted flag
  • Human in the loop required flag (required for high-impact / irreversible actions)

Table 1: Example agent metadata stored in the registry

If any step fails or metrics deteriorate, the deployment stops with logs for root cause analysis. If all checks pass, the agent is packaged and deployed as a containerized workload, producing consistent, reproducible deployments. This prevents ungoverned agents from reaching production, automates compliance checks, and keeps the registry accurate.

At runtime

At runtime, observability has to catch two kinds of drift. Data drift shows up as new or shifting user query patterns, or changes in upstream APIs. Model drift shows as rising error rates or falling tool-selection accuracy. When a customer flags a response, that also triggers an investigation. Alerts for drift, distribution shifts, declining evaluation scores, or direct customer flags prompt a staged response. These events are logged and forwarded to human review. Additionally, teams can run the governance agent continuously to flag drift and operational issues for the responsible team to investigate.

Summary

Building and operating agents at scale is an engineering discipline, not an experimentation exercise.

Effective governance must be structural from the start, externalized, domain-sensitive, and deterministically enforced. We introduced a three-tier composition hierarchy (MCP tools, skills, and flows) as the architectural foundation for reusable, composable, and interoperable agents, decomposed into specialized agents to contain complexity and scope. We showed how verification and evaluation in every CI/CD run make quality assurance part of everyday development, and how defining agent infrastructure as code lets teams apply the same governance rules to every agent in the fleet. Finally, we operationalized these patterns across the agent lifecycle, from pre-validated reference architectures and structured pipelines to a runtime governance agent that continuously evaluates deployed agents.

Our experience has shown these practices pay off in a few ways. Reusable templates and shared infrastructure reduced development costs. Teams also got agents to production faster, thanks to standard interaction models and automated deployment. Quality improved too, because the pipeline enforces proven patterns at every stage of the lifecycle.

Scaling agentic governance is an industry-wide imperative. The shift toward AI and generative-AI-supported workflow automation is already reshaping how engineering organizations operate. The winners will be those who move beyond experimentation and establish the discipline to govern autonomous agent networks at scale. With these practices in place, BMW engineers can focus on solving the problems that matter: Building the ultimate driving machine.

To apply these ideas to your own agents, start with the AWS Well-Architected Framework. This post used it as the model for reusable agent blueprints. To see how BMW codifies governance across its AWS environment, read How BMW Group uses automation to achieve end-to-end compliance at scale on AWS.

Outlook and next steps

The patterns and practices described in this post are a foundation, not a finish line. We are actively extending them across several fronts:

  • Improve architectural guidance: publishing best practice guides on architectural trade-offs, composition patterns, and anti-patterns for teams building agents.
  • Expand infrastructure-as-code templates: providing agent blueprints as usable IaC modules with built-in security and governance standards by default.
  • Deepen governance compliance testing: adding CI/CD test cases verifying governance compliance.
  • Automate standards enforcement: expanding automated checks and managed compliance-scanning rules across pre-deployment and runtime stages.
  • Extend agentic FinOps: Govern the right-sizing of models and tool calls.
  • Agentic user guidance: integrating described patterns into Archimedes, BMW’s architectural guidance agent, to provide contextual architectural recommendations.

Acknowledgements
