entries.summary: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick

Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it.

AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace.

At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use.

Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer.

1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers

Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust.

Quick knows your business, not only your prompts

Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it.

Quick does not stop at your Amazon store

A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone.

It turns data into decisions you can act on

Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it.

Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on

Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays.

The Amazon Selling Partner plugin

The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. The plugin is in beta for US stores.

Figure 1: The Selling Partner plugin consent screen, where the seller grants None, View, or Edit access per data category

The permission screen is worth a pause. The seller grants access per data category, choosing None, View, or Edit for each, and reviews an agreement before authorizing. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and access can be narrowed or revoked later.

2. How to redeem the Quick Plus offer

  • Claim your free AWS Quick Plus subscription (12 months free plus 10 delegated users, by December 31, 2026).
  • Connect the Selling Partner plugin with one sign-in to your Seller Central account. It installs like an app.
  • Ask your first question, something you would normally build a spreadsheet for.

Figure 2: Connecting the Selling Partner plugin from the AWS Quick sign-up flow

3. What the experience looks like

After the plugin is connected, the work happens in a conversation. You ask in plain language, Quick pulls the relevant live data, and it comes back with an answer and a recommended next step. Instead of checking a dashboard, exporting a report, and reconciling it in a spreadsheet, you move from a question to an answer to an action in one place. You review what Quick proposes before anything is sent.

Figure 3: Quick diagnosing whether a sales dip comes from traffic or conversion, using live selling data

4. Two use cases a seller can build

At the Accelerate workshop we had sellers build real agents live, from a plain-language description, in a few minutes. Quick turns the description into a working agent, which the seller then refines in conversation.

Use case A: Inventory Launch Prep

The seller is staging a new product into Amazon and wants the lowest total landed cost. The agent reads supplier data and weighs the fulfillment options per SKU on inbound cost, storage, and speed to sellable. It walks through placement choices and returns the output the seller picks: a shipping plan, a cost comparison, or a combined packet. It explains its reasoning and confirms before it creates anything.

Figure 4: The Inventory Launch Prep agent comparing FBA and AWD fulfillment per factor and recommending a hybrid approach

Use case B: Post-Launch Product Health

After the launch, the agent reads four signal families through the Selling Partner plugin: listing health, inventory, sales, and traffic. It connects them to find the cause rather than just reporting numbers. Flat sales with healthy traffic points to a conversion problem. Flat sales with falling traffic points to discoverability. Good conversion with falling units points to supply. It returns a health summary per ASIN, the diagnosis with evidence, and a ranked fix list, labeling any low-confidence call.

Figure 5: The Post-Launch Product Health agent’s weekly summary, with week-over-week sales evidence

One honest limit, handled honestly: the selling data does not include cost of goods, so the agent reports margin after Amazon fees and labels it that way. When the seller wants true gross margin, the agent asks them to bring their cost numbers into the conversation. It never presents after-fees margin as if it were gross margin.

5. Skills and connectors in action

The Selling Partner plugin and Amazon Ads MCP bring the Amazon selling and advertising data into Quick. Other connectors in AWS Quick bring in the rest of how the business runs, organized by role. These include a second storefront (orders and products from another channel), email and calendar (draft a supplier note, track what is due), team messaging (share an update), and accounting and inventory systems (cost and stock context the selling data does not carry). Because the pieces sit together, the seller can ask one question that reaches across Amazon data and the tools around it.

6. A seller’s morning, start to finish

At Accelerate, Richard Brown, who runs the sneaker care brand Proof Culture and sells across five stores including Amazon, showed what this looks like. He had built his own AI assistant over time, and the hard part was never the AI. It was getting his selling data connected in real time.

“The hard part was never the AI. The hard part was getting my selling data into it, and that is the part that is now simple with the plugin. With Quick and the Selling Partner plugin, just connect your account and start asking questions.”

— Richard Brown, Proof Culture, at Amazon Accelerate 2026

In his demo, Richard asked Quick about upcoming sneaker drops and checked whether he had enough FBA stock to cover a major release. He had Quick model how far his current inventory would carry him. Then he asked it to draft a reorder purchase order and a message to his team. A morning of research across different tools took a few minutes.

7. Getting started

  • Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus (by December 31, 2026).
  • Connect the Selling Partner plugin.
  • Follow the setup instructions to connect the Ads MCP within AWS Quick so you can manage campaigns conversationally alongside your selling data.
  • Connect the rest of your business by role: your other storefront, email and calendar, accounting and inventory systems, team messaging.
  • Start with one real question you would normally handle in a spreadsheet.

Next steps:

Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus

Read the AWS Quick documentation

entries.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints by default and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. It tracks latency, GPU utilization, and serving configuration, then sends a finding through AWS Health with a one-click path to benchmark alternatives in SageMaker Studio before you apply any change.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints

Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it.

Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in  Amazon SageMaker Studio. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings:

  • Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token.
  • Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle.
  • Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use.

SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result.

In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring.

Solution overview

SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action.

  • Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost.
  • Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step.
  • Recommend (opt in) – One selection opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker Studio, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic, so you can benchmark alternatives on separate compute.
  • Decide – Compare response time, throughput, and cost side by side. Production is not changed until you apply a result.

The feature produces a few types of findings. The following table summarizes what triggers each one and what gets tested when you choose to benchmark.

FindingWhat triggers itWhat a benchmark tests
Latency driftResponse time moves relative to the endpoint’s week-over-week trendsTensor parallelism settings and alternate instance types or sizes
Underutilized GPUsGPU utilization stays well below capacity over the windowCheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic
Speculative decoding not enabledModel and container support it, but it is off (configuration based)Current configuration compared to speculative decoding enabled
Serving containerThe endpoint’s serving container has a newer version with a performance improvement and security patches for critical and high finding Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).Current compared to updated container
Untuned GPU kernelsKernel configuration is not tuned for the model and hardwareDefault compared to tuned kernels

Prerequisites

Monitoring itself needs no setup, it is on by default. The following prerequisites apply when you choose to act on a finding by running a benchmark and, optionally, applying a change:

  • Access to AWS Health and the AWS User Notifications console.
  • A SageMaker Studio domain and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to run inference recommendation jobs and update endpoints.
  • Sufficient service quota for the benchmark instances you want to test.

Cost note: Monitoring has no GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges, or your machine learning (ML) reservation if you have one.

Understand a finding notification

You receive notifications in AWS Health on the console and by email and each one follows the same structure, so it’s quick to scan:

  • Endpoint: Which endpoint the finding applies to.
  • What we noticed: The observation, stated plainly, with estimates clearly labeled as estimates.
  • Why it matters: The impact on latency, capacity, or cost.
  • Recommended action: A single selection into the agentic experience in SageMaker Studio to investigate.

Notifications report observations and label estimates. No benchmark has run at this point. A representative notification reads as follows:

Subject: [Action may be required] SageMaker AI inference improvements for your endpoint

SageMaker AI tracks the latency and capacity usage of your inference endpoints by default, and found improvements for one of them. It does not read your requests or responses.

What we noticed: Over the past week, time to first token on this endpoint increased compared with the week before.

Recommended action: Open SageMaker Studio to benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Your production endpoint is not changed.

Cadence: Each endpoint gets one notification that covers the applicable findings. You get at most one notification per endpoint at a time, covering all its findings, and SageMaker AI limits how many an account receives at once. Notifications are AWS Region specific, so you see an endpoint’s findings when you’re signed in to that endpoint’s Region.

Walkthrough: From notification to decision

In this section, we review a few scenarios of endpoint optimizations that will trigger findings to be reported.

Scenario 1: Catch week-over-week latency regression

A team runs a chat assistant on a single SageMaker AI endpoint. They add retrieval to improve answer quality, so every request now carries pages of retrieved context and prompts get much longer. Nothing breaks, and no alarm they set trips, but responses start more slowly.

SageMaker AI compares the endpoint’s median (p50) time to first token and median end-to-end latency with the previous week. When either one rises enough over the week, it flags the change. Because the comparison is against the endpoint’s own history, the team doesn’t need to set a threshold in advance.

  • Notification: AWS Health reports that time to first token increased relative to the prior week.
  • Studio session: One selection opens the agentic experience, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic.
  • Benchmark: The session tests tensor parallelism settings and other instance types or sizes on separate compute.
  • Decision: The team compares latency, throughput, and cost, then applies the winning configuration to one variant.

The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a latency drift finding. The message reports that median time to first token rose about 200 ms week over week, and the Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.

Scenario 2: Turn on an optimization your traffic can benefit from

A platform team hosts an internal code-completion model on a SageMaker AI endpoint. They deployed it with default serving settings and never revisited them. The model and serving container support speculative decoding, a technique for faster responses, but it isn’t enabled. SageMaker AI flags this as an opportunity. Whether it helps depends on the endpoint’s traffic, such as how many requests run concurrently and how long prompts and responses are. The notification recommends running inference recommendations, which benchmarks speculative decoding against the endpoint’s recent traffic and shows whether it’s worth turning on.

  • Notification: AWS Health reports that a technique designed to make responses faster is supported but not enabled.
  • Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint configuration loaded.
  • Benchmark: The session compares the current configuration with speculative decoding enabled. Results may differ at peak compared to off-peak traffic.
  • Decision: If the gain holds at the traffic that matters, the team applies it. Otherwise, they keep the current configuration.

The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding. The message reports that the model and serving container support speculative decoding, but the endpoint doesn’t use it. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.

The notification explains that speculative decoding can make responses faster, and that the benchmark compares response time with and without it on the endpoint’s recent traffic.

Scenario 3: Right-size underutilized GPUs

A summarization endpoint was sized for a launch that drew a fraction of the planned audience, so its GPUs sit mostly idle for a week. This scenario also shows a case where the right decision may be to make no change at all.

  • Notification: AWS Health reports that the endpoint paid for GPU capacity that largely went unused.
  • Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint and its observed peak traffic.
  • Benchmark: The session tests cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic.
  • Decision: The team weighs the monthly savings against the headroom they want for planned growth and may decide to keep the current size.

The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding. The message reports that for most of the week, even the endpoint’s busiest GPU used 12 percent or less of its capacity. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.

You can choose Open in SageMaker AI from the recommended actions as shown in the screenshot above to apply or dismiss a recommendation. Lets walk through this in next section.

Apply or dismiss a recommendation

You stay in control throughout, and nothing deploys automatically. When you choose Open in SageMaker AI from a notification’s recommended actions, Amazon SageMaker Studio opens a JupyterLab space and shows the prompt that will run in the agentic chat. The following screenshot shows the prompt for a latency drift finding on an endpoint that also runs an older vLLM serving container:

When you choose Run, the agentic experience opens in a chat panel in JupyterLab space in SageMaker Studio. It summarizes the finding in plain language, restates what you asked it to do, and checks with you before it takes any action. The following screenshot shows the agent summarizing the findings and asking to continue:

After you confirm, the agent generates a notebook that creates an inference recommendation job for the endpoint. The notebook uses the SageMaker Python SDK, takes the model from the endpoint and the traffic profile from its metrics, and tags the job with the AWS Health event so you can trace the results back to the finding. Each step is a separate notebook cell, so you can review or edit it before you run it.

The following screenshot shows the notebook cells that record the job details and start a recommendation job across three candidate instance types.

When the job completes, you can compare your current configuration with the alternatives on response time, throughput, and cost. When you are ready to act on a benchmarked result, we recommend a safe rollout pattern:

  • Review the proposed change before applying it, including the configuration difference and the benchmarked latency, throughput, and cost.
  • Apply to one production variant first and keep the current configuration available for rollback.
  • Holding or dismissing a finding is a normal outcome. The notification stays in your AWS Health event history.

Manage monitoring and notifications

You can manage monitoring and how you are notified:

  • Manage how you receive notifications in the AWS User Notifications console.
  • Optionally, schedule recurring recommendations, for example monthly.

What is and is not collected: Monitoring reads aggregated latency and capacity telemetry at the endpoint level. It doesn’t read your request or response content, and it carries no GPU cost.

Opting out of monitoring: If you don’t want SageMaker AI to monitor an endpoint, set the 

OPT_OUT_TRACKING
environment variable, with a value of your choice, on the model’s container. You set it in the 
Environment
map when you call 
CreateModel
, either on 
PrimaryContainer
or on another container in the model.

If a container on the endpoint carries this variable, SageMaker AI collects no monitoring telemetry for that endpoint, including engine metrics, GPU metrics, and startup configuration details. As a result, it sends no notifications for that endpoint.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, clean up the resources you created while following this post:

  • Delete any test endpoints or resources you created for the walkthrough.
  • Remove benchmark artifacts in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), if applicable.
  • Revert any test configuration changes you applied.

Conclusion

With SageMaker AI inference recommendations now monitoring your endpoints automatically, optimization moves from a point-in-time snapshot to an ongoing signal.

Your endpoints keep telling you when they have drifted, when they are missing an improvement, or when they are paying for idle capacity. A single selection takes you to a benchmarked, side-by-side decision that you control.

For more information on how to get started, visit Amazon SageMaker AI and see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

entries.title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
entries.summary: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews

For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions?

Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently.

Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths.

We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-led, structured interviewing.

Three core design principles

1. Build interviews around job-related evidence

Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover.

The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience.

2. Separate interviewing from scoring

Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passages.

The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate.

3. Build fairness protections into the design

Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information.

What the research shows

To understand how well these design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency.

Connect Talent keeps interview questions focused on job-relevant skills

The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. Candidates need questions that reflect the requirements of the role, and hiring teams need confidence that the interview assesses those skills.

Amazon engaged an independent I-O psychology firm to evaluate Connect Talent’s AI-generated interview content. The firm reviewed the service’s baseline output before human editing and examined how well its competencies, questions, and rubrics aligned with job requirements. The evaluation found that Connect Talent retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. Of the competencies generated, 91% were clearly traceable to the job description. The firm’s psychologists also found that 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies, and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency.

These findings show that Connect Talent generated job-relevant interview content that met independent expert criteria in a vast majority of cases. Hiring teams can then review, select, and edit the competencies, scorecards, and questions before using them. This human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale.

Connect Talent’s candidate scoring matched independent expert decisions more than 89% of the time

Relevant questions provide the foundation for a structured interview. The next challenge is evaluating the evidence candidates provide with consistency.

To examine this, an independent I-O psychology firm reviewed 36 interviews assessing whether candidates demonstrated specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals.

Connect Talent evaluated the same transcripts, reviewed hundreds of rubric signals, and aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals, which identify behaviors that may indicate a poor fit for the intended role.

The evaluation also produced a Cohen’s kappa of 0.79, a statistical measure that eliminates random chance coincidence. A Cohen’s kappa of 0.79 is just under the standard of 0.81 for almost perfect agreement. This outcome indicates substantial agreement between Connect Talent and the independent expert candidate scoring.

Follow-up questions give candidates more opportunities to demonstrate their strengths

Candidates may have relevant experience but leave important details out of their first response. In a traditional one-way video interview, a candidate may receive a fixed question and have only one opportunity to answer it. Hiring teams must then evaluate the information available, even when the response leaves many important questions unanswered.

Connect Talent uses adaptive follow-ups to gather more complete evidence. For example, a candidate might describe improving a slow system. The AI interviewer can ask what changed, which actions the candidate took, and how they measured the improvement. These questions help candidates explain their contributions and results in greater detail.

We studied the impact of follow-up questions by comparing assessments based on a candidate’s first response with assessments based on the full interview conversation. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Assessments using the full conversation also came closer to expert evaluations.

Without follow-up questions, the scoring process identified fewer strength signals and more concern signals. In some cases, the candidate’s initial response simply lacked the information needed to demonstrate a relevant behavior. The full conversation captured more of what candidates demonstrated and gave hiring teams a more complete record of their experience.

Structured scoring helps hiring teams recognize meaningful differences

Hiring teams need scores that reflect meaningful differences in demonstrated skills. Yet research has found that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making those differences harder to recognize (Zhu et al., 2026).

Connect Talent uses behaviorally anchored scorecards to evaluate specific strength and concern signals. Rather than asking an AI model to assign an overall rating, the service identifies evidence for each behavior and calculates the competency score using a predefined formula.

Consider the competency “collaboration”. A general AI scoring approach might evaluate a candidate’s overall collaboration skills based on the interview transcript. Connect Talent examines specific behaviors, such as whether the candidate sought input from colleagues before making a decision. Each finding contributes to the final score.

We evaluated this approach across hundreds of expert-rated interview assessments. Connect Talent’s structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points.

This wider distribution allows the scoring system to represent more levels of demonstrated competency. The behaviorally anchored scorecards also help hiring teams understand the evidence behind each rating.

Bringing hiring science to AI-led interviews

Connect Talent brings the rigor of structured interviewing to more people while giving each candidate a meaningful chance to demonstrate their skills. The result is a new opportunity for organizations hiring at scale: more candidates can show what they can do, and more hiring teams can make decisions grounded in the evidence that matters.

Learn More at AWS re:Invent 2026

Join us at AWS re:Invent 2026 for BIZ332: Every Candidate, Every Time: AI-Led Structured Interviews with Amazon Connect Talent, an interactive Chalk Talk led by Sunitha Srivatsa and Gerald Friedland.

The session will explore the science behind Connect Talent, including structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions, and evidence-based scoring.

Session 1: Monday, November 30, 2026, 10:00–11:00 AM, Caesars Forum – Level 1, Academy 409.

Repeat session: Thursday, December 3, 2026, 3:00–4:00 PM, MGM Grand, Premier 309.

entries.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness now runs on the open-source Strands harness, bringing a recommended model, task-oriented defaults, automatic prompt caching, proactive context management, and new built-in tools. It also adds lifecycle hooks so you can run deterministic allow or deny checks at defined points in the agent loop.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks

When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

Strands capabilities, on AWS

Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself.

You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability.

AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment.

A more capable managed harness

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:

  • A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence.
  • Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior.
  • Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost.
  • Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses.
  • Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context usage without losing access to the data.
  • Planning across invocations. The 
    todo_write
    tool maintains a structured task plan that can be restored in later invocations within the same session, including after conversation summarization.
  • Focused delegation. The 
    subagent
    tool delegates a self-contained task to a fresh worker and returns the result to the parent agent. The worker is internal to the invocation, not a separately managed harness resource, and shares invocation limits and your tool-call lifecycle hooks.
  • Web retrieval. The 
    web_fetch
    tool retrieves content from a specified webpage to give your harness up-to-date external context.
  • Granular filesystem access. With separate 
    read
    , 
    write
    , and 
    edit
    tools, you can grant only the granular filesystem capabilities an agent needs.

Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.

Recommended by default, configurable when needed

Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve.

Explicit configuration always takes precedence:

  • Configure a model ID to keep using a specific model.
  • Configure 
    systemPrompt
    to completely replace the managed system prompt.
  • Configure 
    truncation
    to keep a specific context-management policy.
  • List individual 
    allowedTools
    selectors to maintain a fixed tool surface.

When 

allowedTools
is omitted or set to 
["*"]
, Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need.

For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification:

Govern consequential actions with lifecycle hooks

With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow.

Harness supports four lifecycle events:

EventWhen it runsEffect of a Lambda denial
before_invocation
 Before the agent processes the requestStops the invocation with 
hook_stopped
 
before_tool_call
 After the model proposes a tool call and before executionSkips the tool call. The agent loop continues
after_tool_call
 After a tool result existsRetains the result and stops before further inference
after_invocation
 After the invocation completesReports the decision. Output already streamed cannot be retracted

Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop.

For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a 

before_tool_call
hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness:

The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision:

When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the 

InvokeHarness
response stream as a 
hookEvent
:

Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same 

beforeToolCall
and 
afterToolCall
hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (
beforeInvocation
, 
afterInvocation
) run once for the whole invocation.

You configure hooks with 

CreateHarness
or 
UpdateHarness
. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its 
failureMode
, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.

To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between 

failureMode
deny and allow.

Run a multi-agent research coordinator with the AgentCore CLI

Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself.

The 

agentcore harness
commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm:

The CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no 

--profile
flag, so set the 
AWS_PROFILE
environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as 
system_prompt.md
in your working directory.

Create the harness

This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you.

Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print 

READY
:

Send the prompts

Invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents:

Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator plans the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment.

With 

--prompt
, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out 
--prompt
, and the CLI opens an interactive chat.

The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub.

Clean up

Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass 

--delete-managed-memory false
. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it.

Rollout and compatibility

On November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required.

Configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or 

truncation
configuration, or use 
allowedTools: ["*"]
, receive the upgraded managed defaults.

If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly.

Learn more

Create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior.

  • Strands harness announcement.
  • Get started with AgentCore harness.
  • Managed system prompt.
  • AgentCore harness API reference.
  • Lifecycle hooks.
  • Refund Desk lifecycle hooks code sample.

We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness.

entries.title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
entries.summary: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of recordings from a consenting speaker, and it builds a custom voice that reads new text in that speaker's voice. Cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine and support seven languages.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices.

Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details.

Hear it for yourself

Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded.

  • From recordings to TTS voice. A few minutes of our science lead Trevor’s source audio, and the resulting generative voice.
    • Recorded: “Hello, I’m Trevor, from Science.” Cloned voice: “That first sentence was my real voice. This is my cloned voice, created from a few minutes of my recordings. It can read any text you give it.”
  • Supports seven languages. Hear Jonas, one of the authors, speaking German in his recording and then in his cloned voice:
    • Recorded: “Hallo, ich bin Jonas. Das ist meine echte Stimme.” (Hi, I’m Jonas. This is my real voice.) Cloned voice: “Und das ist meine geklonte Stimme! Gleiche Stimme, neue Worte: Diesen Satz habe ich geschrieben, aber nie aufgenommen.” (And this is my cloned voice! Same voice, new words: I wrote this sentence, but never recorded it.)
  • Use in a variety of applications. Here’s Trevor in a new job he hasn’t had: a non-player character in a game.
    • “Who’s that crossing my bridge? Oh, it’s you again. Same deal as last time: answer my riddle, or hand over the sandwich.”
  • Expand your voice library with voice cloning. Hear this audio sample from AWS Chief Evangelist Jeff Barr: a real recording, then his cloned voice.
    • Recorded: “Hi, I’m Jeff, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “And this is how my cloned voice sounds, reading a sentence I never recorded.”
  • Hannah: a real recording, then her cloned voice on a support line.
    • Recorded: “Hello, I’m Hannah. This is my real voice.” Cloned voice: “Thanks for calling AnyCompany. Your order 4471 9902 ships today and should arrive on Thursday between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.”
  • Joely: a real recording, then her cloned voice narrating a lesson.
    • Recorded: “Hi, I’m Joely, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “In this module, we’ll look at how a neural network learns. First, it makes a guess. Then it measures how far off that guess was, and adjusts, a little at a time.”

What you can build

A consistent brand voice across channels

Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel.

Contact centers

Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences.

Media and content at scale

Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates quickly.

Localization with a consistent persona

Maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language.

Accessibility and personalization

Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice.

How voice cloning works

With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice:

A cloned voice goes through four steps:

  • Record. You record one speaker (see the following recording tips). You can send the recordings directly in the 
    CreateVoice
    request or upload them on the console. You can also store them in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the AWS Region where you want the voice and point Amazon Polly to them.
  • Create. You call 
    CreateVoice
    with 1-10 recordings, the language they are spoken in, and 
    TermsAccepted=True
    , your confirmation that you have the speaker’s consent. Amazon Polly returns a voice ID (
    vc-…
    ) right away and builds the voice in the background.
  • Wait. Creation is asynchronous and typically takes 5-10 minutes. During that time, Amazon Polly also checks the quality of your text-to-speech (TTS) voice for speaker similarity. You call 
    GetVoice
    until the status changes from 
    pending
    to 
    active
    or 
    failed
    .
  • Use. You pass the voice ID to 
    SynthesizeSpeech
    for real-time audio or to 
    StartSpeechSynthesisTask
    for long-form audio written to S3, with 
    Engine="generative"
    , the same way you call the other generative voices in Amazon Polly. When you no longer need the voice, you call 
    DeleteVoice
    .

Consent and control

A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted.

  • You confirm consent for each voice you create. When you create a voice, on the console or with 
    TermsAccepted=True
    in the API, you confirm that you have obtained all rights and consents necessary to create and use the cloned voice. Your use of voice cloning is subject to the AWS Service Terms, the Biometric Notice and Consent Terms, the AWS Responsible AI Policy, and the AWS Acceptable Use Policy.
  • Generated speech carries a watermark. Amazon Polly adds a watermark to text-to-speech audio generated with the cloned voice.
  • Only your account can use it. A cloned voice is scoped to the AWS account that created it, and you control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You can encrypt voices with your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and tag them.
  • You decide when it goes away. Delete a voice with one 
    DeleteVoice
    call or on the console, once it’s active or its creation has failed.
  • Amazon Polly does not retain a copy of your voice recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data it needs to synthesize speech, and stores it encrypted. You can use your own AWS KMS key for that encryption, and 
    DeleteVoice
    removes the data immediately.

We recommend that you:

  • Keep a record of each speaker’s consent.
  • Delete the voice if the speaker withdraws consent.
  • Tell listeners when they’re hearing a synthetic voice where that’s appropriate.
  • Grant voice permissions only to the people and systems that need them.

For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance.

Best practices for recordings

Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter.

  • Record two to ten minutes of natural speech, split into takes of up to a minute. You can send up to 10 recordings per voice, and up to 15 minutes of audio in total. Quality matters more than length: more audio might not change how the voice sounds.
  • One speaker, a quiet room, the same distance from the mic. Use a USB microphone, or a phone app that can record WAV. Record in mono WAV, 16-bit, at 24 kHz from the start, so there’s nothing to convert later. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats, but we recommend WAV. See the Amazon Polly Developer Guide for supported formats and limits.
  • Avoid using meeting apps and browser recorders. Their echo cancellation and noise suppression change the voice, and the clone learns those changes too.
  • Record every take in the style you want the voice to have. The cloned voice takes its style from the recordings and can’t blend several, so upbeat, sad, and angry takes won’t give you a voice that can do all three.
  • Record in the language the voice should speak. Voice cloning is tested with recordings in US English, German, US Spanish, French, Italian, Brazilian Portuguese, and Hindi. Recordings in other accents of these languages, such as British English or Canadian French, also work but are less tested, so check the voice with your own content.

Getting started

On the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page.

In code, you need:

  • The latest version of boto3 (
    pip install --upgrade boto3
    ).
  • IAM permissions for 
    polly:CreateVoice
    , 
    polly:GetVoice
    , 
    polly:DescribeVoices
    , 
    polly:SynthesizeSpeech
    and 
    polly:DeleteVoice
    . For long-form audio, also 
    polly:StartSpeechSynthesisTask
    , 
    polly:GetSpeechSynthesisTask
    and 
    s3:PutObject
    on the output bucket.
  • For the following Amazon S3 example: your recordings in a bucket in the Region where you create the voice, with 
    s3:GetObject
    permission for the IAM role or user that calls 
    CreateVoice
    .

If Python reports that the 

Polly
object has no attribute 
create_voice
, upgrade boto3.

For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3:

For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo.

Production considerations

Create voices ahead of time

Voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call 

CreateVoice
, check 
GetVoice
every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. 
CreateVoice
and 
DeleteVoice
share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions.

Keep an inventory

DescribeVoices
lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have 
Origin
set to 
customer
. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique 
Name
. If a 
CreateVoice
call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check 
DescribeVoices
for that name before you try again.

Plan for errors

CreateVoice
returns 
ThrottlingException
when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with 
DeleteVoice
, and 
ServiceQuotaExceededException
when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns 
ConflictException
. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, 
StatusReason
gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a new one.

Scope permissions to voices

Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep 

polly:CreateVoice
and 
polly:DeleteVoice
for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role:

With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using 

aws:ResourceTag
conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows 
polly:SynthesizeSpeech
on all resources (
"Resource": "*"
) also covers every cloned voice in the account.

Plan for quotas and Regions

Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy.

Test with your real scripts

Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML)

tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags.

Things to know

AvailabilityAccess is enabled per AWS account. If you see Voice cloning in the Amazon Polly console (expand the left panel and see if Voice cloning is listed), it’s enabled for your account. If not, you can reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to request access. Supported AWS Regions are the same as the generative engine: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). A cloned voice lives in the AWS Region where you created it.
LanguagesEnglish, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Tested recording locales: US English (
en-US
), German (
de-DE
), US Spanish (
es-US
), French (
fr-FR
), Italian (
it-IT
), Brazilian Portuguese (
pt-BR
), and Hindi (
hi-IN
). Other accents of these languages also work but are less tested. Each voice speaks the language it was recorded in.
Recordings1-10 recordings per voice, up to 15 minutes in total. WAV is recommended: mono, 16-bit, at 24 kHz or 44.1/48 kHz. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats too. Console uploads are limited to 5 MB per file. For larger files, use Amazon S3.
Data handlingAmazon Polly deletes its copy of your recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data needed for synthesis, stored encrypted (you can use your own AWS KMS key), until you call 
DeleteVoice
.
Creation timeTypically takes 5-10 minutes to build a TTS voice, asynchronous.
Synthesis latencySame as Generative voices in Amazon Polly.
Quotas10 cloned voices per account per AWS Region initially. To request an increase, contact AWS Support. 
CreateVoice
and 
DeleteVoice
share a limit of 1 request per second.
SynthesisCloned voices follow the Amazon Polly quotas for generative voices, including the text limits per request and per synthesis task. See Amazon Polly quotas.
PricingCreating a cloned voice is free. Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis. See Amazon Polly pricing.
APIs
CreateVoice
, 
GetVoice
, 
DeleteVoice
and 
DescribeVoices
to manage voices. 
SynthesizeSpeech
and 
StartSpeechSynthesisTask
with 
Engine="generative"
to use them. See the Amazon Polly API reference.

Conclusion

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

For the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo.

We can’t wait to hear what you build.

Thanks to Trevor Wood, Jonas Rohnke, Suyin Wang, Hannah Barrett, Nikie Xiong, Jeff Barr, and Joely Huang for lending us their voices.

entries.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
entries.summary: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend can grow even as per-token prices fall. This post walks through six composable optimization levers, shows how Accenture applied them across four client engagements, and recommends a sequence for cutting AI token spend on your own workloads.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.

In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.

Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.

Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level

Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.

Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.

Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.

The six optimization levers

The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.

Phase 1: Configuration only, no infrastructure change

With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).

Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.

Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes.

Phase 2: Architectural changes

Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.

Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.

Phase 3: Infrastructure and training investment

Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers.

Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.

In production: Four client engagements

Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.

The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.

The second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.

The third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.

Results

Outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.

These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.

Production governance: Four operating tenets

Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.

These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.

Getting started

You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.

The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.
